entities.name: Leonteus of Lampsacus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Leonteus of Lampsacus, a devoted pupil of the renowned philosopher Epicurus, was a significant figure in the early development and propagation of Epicurean thought during the Hellenistic period, specifically active in the early 3rd century BCE until his death in 201 BCE. His importance lies not in original philosophical treatises, but in his unwavering adherence to Epicurus's teachings and his role in establishing a familial legacy within the philosophical school, thereby embodying the communal and personal aspects central to Epicureanism. As a resident of Lampsacus, an Ionian city on the Hellespont, Leonteus participated in the vibrant intellectual exchanges that characterized the post-Alexandrian Greek world, connecting regional centers with the Athenian intellectual hub.

Leonteus joined Epicurus's school, known as The Garden, in Athens, where he absorbed the core tenets of Epicurean philosophy, which prioritized ataraxia (freedom from disturbance) and aponia (absence of pain) through rational living and friendship. His commitment was famously demonstrated through his marriage to Themista, a fellow student of Epicurus, a remarkable instance of gender inclusivity within an ancient philosophical institution. Their shared intellectual pursuit and personal bond culminated in a profound gesture of reverence for their master: they named their son Epicurus, ensuring the philosopher's name echoed through their lineage and symbolizing the deep personal impact of the school's founder.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Leonteus of Lampsacus holds significance primarily as a devoted pupil who, alongside his wife Themista, exemplified the personal and familial integration of Epicurean philosophy, thereby contributing to the school's living legacy and demonstrating its appeal beyond purely academic circles. His actions helped to transmit and normalize Epicurean ideals within society.
